Abstract

Objective: Many individuals with rheumatic disease are at higher risk for severe acute COVID-

19. We aimed to evaluate risk factors for Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) using an

electronic health record (EHR)-based definition.

Methods: We identified patients with prevalent rheumatic diseases and COVID-19 at Mass

General Brigham. PASC was defined by ICD codes, relevant labs, vital signs, and medications,

at least 30 days following the first COVID-19 infection. Patients were followed until the earliest

of incident PASC, repeat COVID-19 infection, 1 year of follow-up, death, or February 19, 2023.

We used multivariable Cox regression to estimate the association of baseline characteristics

with PASC risk.

Results: Among 2,459 patients (76.37% female, mean age 57.4 years), the most common

incident PASC manifestations were cough (14.56%), dyspnea (12.36%), constipation (11.39%),

and fatigue (10.70%). Serious manifestations including acute coronary disease (4.43%),

thromboembolism (3.09%), hypoxemia (3.09%), stroke (1.75%), and myocarditis (0.12%) were

rare. The Delta wave (aHR 0.63, 95% CI: 0.49-0.82) and Omicron era (aHR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41-

0.62) were associated with lower risk of PASC than the early pandemic (March 2020-June

2021). Age, obesity, comorbidity burden, race, and hospitalization for acute COVID-19 infection

were associated with greater risk of PASC.

Conclusion: Among patients with rheumatic diseases, following their first COVID-19 infection,

using an EHR-based definition, we found a decreased risk of PASC over calendar time. Aside

from glucocorticoids, no specific immunomodulatory medications were associated with

increased risk, and risk factors were otherwise similar to those seen in the general population.

## Introduction

Patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) often use

immunosuppressive medications that can increase the risk of severe acute outcomes of

coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).[1-5] They are also made more vulnerable by blunted

immune response to the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines.[6-14] Additionally, immune dysregulation and

predisposition to autoantibody formation and fibrosis may also contribute to worse COVID-19

outcomes.[15] Whether SARDs and their treatments contribute to an increased risk of post-acute

sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) is unclear.

“Long Covid,” or PASC has been defined in various ways. Some definitions characterize

PASC as any persistent symptom at a specified duration (e.g., one month, three months, or

other time interval) following acute COVID-19 infection.[16-18] More recent definitions have been

based on the presence of specific patient-reported symptoms.[16,19,20] Some have restricted the

definition to the occurrence of specific severe manifestations such as thrombosis, neuropathy,

new-onset diabetes, or other new chronic comorbidity. Using patient-reported symptoms, we

previously found that approximately 50% of patients with SARDs experience PASC after an

acute COVID-19 infection.[21] Several studies in the general population have evaluated PASC

using an electronic health record (EHR)-based definition. Little is known about the burden and

characteristics of EHR-based definitions of PASC, or its risk factors, in patients with SARDs.

EHR-based definitions of PASC and those based on self-report provide complementary

perspectives on the post-acute consequences of COVID-19. Patient-reported outcomes provide

important insights into the patient experience and frequently capture manifestations of PASC

that clinicians may be unaware of and that are unlikely to be documented in clinical notes or as

encounter claims. In contrast, EHR-based definitions of PASC capture symptoms prompting

medical encounters as well as features that may only be diagnosed by a clinician based on

physical exam, laboratory testing, imaging, and other diagnostics.

## Methods

Study population and SARD patient identification

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating factors associated with PASC

among patients with SARDs at Mass General Brigham (MGB). MGB is a large, multi-center

healthcare system that includes two tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital

and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), twelve community hospitals, and their associated primary

and specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts, area. We identified

people who were seen within MGB who were ≥18 years of age, had a positive test result for

SARS-CoV-2 by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen nasopharyngeal test between

March 1, 2020 and January 18, 2023 using the MGB centralized data warehouse, Research

Patient Data Registry (RPDR), and had a rheumatic disease diagnosis based on International

Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 code. Diagnosis of a SARD was then confirmed by manual

review of the EHR. This approach has been previously described.[1,3] We also required that

patients have a visit within the MGB healthcare system between one and three years prior to the

index date to identify those with a history of engagement in MGB. The first documented SARS-

CoV-2 infection was used as the index date (Figure 1). This study was approved by the MGB

Institutional Review Board (2020P000833).

Ascertainment of potential risk factors and covariates

Patient demographics, rheumatic disease history, COVID-19 vaccine history, and details

of their acute COVID-19 infection (including date, symptoms, and severity) were ascertained by

manual review of the EHR. Calendar time of acute COVID-19 was divided into three categories:

March 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021 during which the Alpha strain was dominant, July 1-

December 16, 2021 during which the Delta strains were dominant, and December 17, 2021 (at

which point Omicron became the dominant strain locally) through January 18, 2023 (the latest

index date in our study).[23]

Baseline comorbidities as defined by ICD-10 codes, smoking history, and body mass

index (BMI) were obtained from RPDR and assessed in the one year prior to the index date.

The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was calculated using ICD-10 data collected in the one

year prior to the index date.

To categorize patients into a single medication group in the Cox regression models, we

used a previously described[24] hierarchical system, regardless of the number of medications

they were prescribed, as follows: CD20 inhibitor, cyclophosphamide, tumor necrosis factor

(TNF) inhibitor, IL-6 receptor inhibitor, cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4

immunoglobulin (CTLA-4 Ig), IL-17 inhibitor/IL-23 inhibitor/IL-12/23 inhibitor, other biologic

disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (bDMARD), targeted synthetic DMARD (tsDMARD)/Janus

kinase (JAK) inhibitor, mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolic acid, methotrexate, and other

csDMARD, with antimalarial monotherapy as a reference group.

Outcome Assessment: PASC

The primary outcome was PASC, defined by any incident post-acute sequelae with no

record of the particular qualifying sequelae in the one year prior to the index date. Encounter,

procedure, and medication data to define incident PASC were extracted from RPDR. In

particular, ICD-10 codes and prescription medications were ascertained in the one year prior to

COVID-19 infection, and laboratory values and vital signs were ascertained in the five years

prior to COVID-19 infection.

Post-acute sequelae were defined by ICD-10 codes, laboratory values (low-density

lipoprotein, triglycerides, hemoglobin A1c, creatinine), body mass index, and/or medications (for

glucose control, lipid metabolism, cough, anxiety, or sleep). This definition was adapted from the

one used by Al-Aly et al.[22] The qualifying ICD codes, laboratory, and vital parameters, and

medications used to identify features (or criterion) of PASC are outlined in Supplementary

Statistical analysis

Categorical variables are presented as number (percentage), and continuous variables

are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median ± interquartile range, as appropriate.

The index date was defined as the date of the first documented infection with SARS-CoV-2.

Patients were followed from 30 days after the index date (to identify features of PASC persisting

beyond or developing after the acute infection) until the earliest date of: 1) death, 2) a

subsequent COVID-19 infection (a minimum of 60 days following the index date, to avoid

capturing repeat positive testing from the initial infection), 3) 12 months following the index date,

or 4) the end of the study period (February 19, 2023), and person-months of follow-up were

determined for each patient.

We assessed the association of factors of interest among SARD patients with the risk of

PASC using unadjusted and multivariable Cox regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HR)

and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The multivariable model was adjusted for age, sex, CCI,

and vaccination status (unvaccinated or partially vaccinated, fully vaccinated based on the initial

definition of 2 mRNA vaccines or 1 Johnson & Johnson/Janssen vaccine, or additional vaccines

beyond the primary vaccination series), and calendar time as described above. Because

hospitalization due to COVID-19 infection occurs after the index date and may be a mediator of

observed associations, it was not included as a covariate.

To assess the robustness of our results, we performed several subgroup and sensitivity

analyses. First, we limited the population to those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) to limit potential

for confounding by indication for medications. Second, we performed an additional multivariable

analysis that adjusted for immunosuppressive medication class (when evaluating the

We also assessed differences in PASC criteria between those with RA, systemic lupus

We assessed for proportional hazards assumption by including an interaction term

met in all analyses. The level of significance was set as a two-sided p<0.05. We did not adjust

for multiple comparisons. Statistical analyses were completed using SAS statistical software

(version 9.4; SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC).

## Results

Participant Characteristics

We analyzed 2,459 patients with SARDs and COVID-19 (Table 1). The majority of

patients were female (76.37%). The mean (SD) age at time of COVID-19 was 57.4 (16.6) years

and 1,862 (75.72%) were White. The median (IQR) Charlson Comorbidity Index was 1.0 (1.0-

3.0). The most common SARD category was RA (815, 33.14%), followed by other inflammatory

arthritis (561, 22.81%), SLE (268, 10.90%), giant cell arteritis and/or polymyalgia rheumatica

(157, 6.38%), and AAV (134, 5.45%). The most common conventional synthetic DMARDs used

at the time of COVID-19 were methotrexate (591, 24.03%), antimalarials (540, 21.96%), and

mycophenolate (152, 6.18%). The most common biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs at

the time of COVID-19 included TNF inhibitors (556, 22.61%) followed by CD20 inhibitors (174,

7.08%) and JAK inhibitors (84, 3.42%).

At baseline, many patients had features that are used to define PASC in the one year

prior to the index date (Supplementary Table 3). The organ systems or categories with the

most prevalent conditions at baseline were endocrine (70.03%), musculoskeletal (61.29%),

gastrointestinal (38.19%), pulmonary (37.62%), and mental health (37.29%). The most common

prevalent individual manifestations were joint pain (61.04%), hyperlipidemia (52.83%), obesity

(45.87%), cough (28.67%), anxiety (28.30%), and constipation (24.68%).

In our study sample, there were 9,323 person-months of follow-up. During this time,

there were 1,412 people who developed PASC, yielding an incidence rate of 151.5 (95% CI:

143.6-159.4) per 1,000 person-months. Following acute COVID-19, the proportion with any

incident PASC criteria during the follow-up period was 57.42% (Supplementary Table 4). The

most common organ systems involved were cardiovascular (23.51%), followed by pulmonary

(23.34%), gastrointestinal (20.17%), mental health (14.88%), and renal (13.34%) (Figure 2).

The most common individual PASC manifestations were cough (14.56%), shortness of breath

(12.36%), constipation (11.39%), fatigue (10.70%), chest pain (10.00%), anxiety (9.56%), and

acute kidney injury (9.52%). Potentially serious manifestations including acute coronary disease

(4.43%), thromboembolism (3.09%), hypoxemia (3.09%), stroke (1.75%), and myocarditis

(0.12%) were uncommon though notable. The proportion with PASC decreased over calendar

time, from 80.24% in the early pandemic, to 58.33% during the Delta wave, to 44.11% during

the Omicron era.

When compared to patients with RA, those with SLE and AAV more often experienced

cardiovascular (23.07% in RA compared to 30.22% in SLE and 30.60% in AAV), dermatologic

(6.38% in RA vs. 10.82% in SLE and 9.70% in AAV), and renal (12.02% in RA vs. 17.16% in

SLE and 15.67% in AAV) manifestations of PASC. Thromboembolism (2.94% in RA vs. 2.99%

in SLE vs. 5.97% in AAV) and hypoxemia (2.33% in RA vs. 0.37% in SLE and 10.45% in AAV)

were most common in AAV, whereas neurologic and mental health manifestations including

anxiety (7.73% in RA vs. 12.69% in SLE and 5.97% in AAV) and headache (5.28% in RA vs.

Baseline factors associated with the risk of PASC

During the follow-up period, there were 441 patients who developed PASC by our

diagnostic criteria. Age (aHR 1.05 per 10 years, 95% CI: 1.02-1.09), obesity (aHR 1.29

compared to normal body mass index, 95% CI: 1.12-1.48 compared to normal weight), greater

comorbidity burden (aHR 1.10 per unit increase in CCI, 95% CI: 1.08-1.12), Black race (aHR

1.35, 95% CI: 1.13-1.62 compared to White race), and hospitalization for acute COVID-19

infection (aHR 1.34 compared to no hospitalization, 95% CI: 1.16-1.56) were associated with

greater risk of PASC (Table 2). Infections occurring during the Delta wave (aHR 0.63, 95% CI:

0.49-0.82) and Omicron era (aHR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41-0.62) were each associated with lower

risk of PASC than the early pandemic (Figure 3A). There was no association of sex, smoking

status, ethnicity, or vaccination status with risk of PASC in adjusted analyses.

Patients with SLE (aHR 1.44, 95% CI: 1.19-1.74) and AAV (aHR 1.28, 95% CI: 1.01-

1.63) had a higher risk of PASC than patients with RA (Figure 3B). Compared to those

receiving antimalarial monotherapy, patients prescribed TNF inhibitors (aHR 0.72, 95% CI: 0.59-

0.87), IL-6 receptor inhibitors (aHR 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.91), CTLA-4 Ig (aHR 0.59, 95% CI:

0.39-0.93), and methotrexate (aHR 0.78, 95% CI: 0.63-0.96) had a lower risk of PASC. There

was no association of CD20 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or other csDMARDs with risk of PASC.

Systemic glucocorticoid use was associated with greater risk of PASC (aHR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.05-

1.34) compared with no use.

Subgroup and sensitivity analyses

In the subgroup analysis evaluating risk of PASC among patients only with RA, age,

obesity, comorbidity burden, past smoking status, and hospitalization for acute COVID-19

infection all remained associated with higher risk of PASC (Supplementary Table 5). COVID-

19 infection during the Delta wave and Omicron era was associated with lower PASC risk

## Discussion

In this retrospective cohort study of individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 extending

through the Omicron era, we found that the prevalence of PASC using an EHR-based definition

was high. However, we observed a significant decrease in the risk of PASC over calendar time,

perhaps due to differences in variants and availability of vaccines. Among those with SARDs,

we found higher risk of PASC in those with SLE and AAV compared to those with RA, with the

association of SLE with PASC persisting even after adjusting for specific immunomodulatory

medication use. Certain baseline factors (e.g., age, obesity, comorbidity burden, race,

hospitalization for acute COVID-19 infection) associated with PASC in people with SARDs were

similar to those observed in the general population. Our study is the first to leverage an EHR-

based definition of PASC in people with SARDs. A strength of using an EHR-based definition in

contrast to a definition based solely on patient symptoms is that we are able assess these

clinically relevant endpoints.

There has been particular concern regarding whether people with SARDs may be more

vulnerable to PASC due to immunosuppression, a predisposition to autoimmunity, fibrosis,

and/or dysregulated immunity, an impaired response to SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, or because they

have more severe acute COVID-19 infection.[21,25,26] We found high rates of PASC in this

vulnerable population but this burden was not distributed equally across all of the organ systems

in which features of PASC were assessed. Features of PASC affecting the cardiovascular,

pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems were most commonly observed in this population,

while others, such as the musculoskeletal, dermatologic, and coagulation domains were less

commonly affected. In part, this may reflect the frequency with which some manifestations of

PASC were prevalent in this population prior to their COVID-19 infection. However, this also

highlights important directions for future analyses focused on refining the definition of PASC in

this population and identifying opportunities for intervention.

In the general population, risk factors for PASC have included older age, greater

comorbidity burden, obesity, belonging to a racial or ethnic minority, female sex, and

hospitalization for or more severe acute COVID-19 clinical course.[27-29] Indeed, we found similar

risk factors in this study in patients with rheumatic diseases.[27,30] With regard to rheumatic

disease-specific risk factors for PASC, though studies have found that longer duration of

autoimmune disease may be associated with greater risk, we hypothesized that differences in

immunomodulatory treatments would predispose to different risks of PASC.[26,27,31] However, we

did not find consistent associations of use of certain immunomodulators with PASC as we have

in other studies of COVID-19, particularly in the acute setting.[24] The COVAD study utilized a

questionnaire in patients with SARDs to evaluate the risk of PASC as defined by patient-

reported symptoms and also found no specific risk by DMARD treatment.[27]

We found an association of a diagnosis of SLE and AAV with a higher risk of PASC. One

possible explanation for this finding is that the definition of PASC includes features of these

conditions. Therefore, the observed association suggests that flare in SLE and AAV may be an

important post-acute complication of COVID-19. Indeed, we included patients who were users

of the system prior to the index date, and we excluded features from meeting PASC criteria if

they were prevalent within one year prior to the index date. Thus, we have identified incident

occurrences of these conditions following the index date. Findings including greater degree of

dermatologic and renal manifestations in these populations compared to RA, and findings of

higher proportion with neurologic manifestations in SLE and pulmonary manifestations in AAV

suggest that the rheumatic disease may be flaring given that these organ systems are

frequently affected in these diseases (Supplementary Table 4). Risk of incident SLE and

vasculitis may be greater following COVID-19 infection, but whether COVID-19 exacerbates

underlying rheumatic disease is under-studied.[25,32] Our findings also suggest that the factors

contributing to PASC may differ across diseases. When adjusting for specific

immunomodulatory medication, AAV was no longer significantly associated with PASC,

whereas SLE still was. This suggests that medication use may be a factor in the risk of PASC

among people with AAV but that the pathway to PASC in SLE may be different. Further work is

needed to elucidate the pathways driving an association between COVID-19 and PASC in

people with rheumatic diseases and whether disease flares following infection may be

contributing.

In unadjusted analyses, we found that vaccination was associated with a lower risk of

PASC, as we observed in previous earlier studies of the same cohort and as had been

described elsewhere. This finding did not persist in adjusted analyses but these included

calendar time as a covariate which is closely linked with vaccination status. The improvement in

the risk of PASC over calendar time observed in our study is likely multifactorial and may be

related to differences and decreased virulence of the Omicron variant compared to earlier

strains, increased vaccination over time, the availability of treatments for COVID-19, and other

factors. This finding is consistent with those observed in the general population regarding the

decline in risk of PASC over time.[33] Determining whether PASC may continue to decline over

time and whether emphasis on maintaining up-to-date SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates over time

may contribute to an ongoing decline in PASC risk moving forward warrants further study.

Our study has multiple strengths. First, we systematically identified a large sample of

people with SARDs and COVID-19 infection, both confirmed by manual medical record review.

Second, due to the combination of comprehensive data from our registry as well as from MGB’s

data warehouse, we were able to ascertain key patient and disease-specific features, including

comorbidities, rheumatic disease and related medications, and details of their COVID-19

infection and vaccination history. Third, we leveraged a comprehensive EHR-based definition of

PASC, encompassing ICD-10 codes, medications, laboratory values, and vital signs. Use of

administrative data is helpful for a population estimate of PASC prevalence and risk factors

since it is not dependent on willingness to participate in a prospective research study and

captures multiple facets of PASC, including symptoms (e.g., fatigue, shortness of breath) and

objective findings (e.g., deep vein thrombosis, diabetes). Fourth, our group has continued to

systematically identify people throughout the pandemic, creating a dataset that encompasses

those with COVID-19 infections ranging from the early pandemic through the recent Omicron

era.

Our study also has limitations. First, our use of an EHR-based definition of PASC did not

require attribution of symptoms to COVID-19 infection. The prevalence of PASC may be

overestimated in our study, though other studies with similar broad definitions, whether EHR or

patient questionnaire based, have also demonstrated prevalence of PASC of >50%. Our study

design required that all patients were actively engaged in the MGB healthcare system to limit

potential for differences by ascertainment. In future studies, alternative study designs that use a

comparator group (e.g., SARD patients without COVID-19 infection, SARD patients following

influenza vaccination, or general population comparators following COVID-19 infection) should

be pursued. Despite this limitation, our study establishes important benchmarks and identifies

directions for future studies of PASC in this vulnerable and under-studied population. Second,

our use of ICD-10 codes as opposed to patient questionnaires has the potential to

underestimate certain criteria (e.g., anosmia, fatigue) that may not be reported to providers.

a patient may report as well as those that may be diagnosed by a clinician.

In summary, we established important benchmarks in the risk of PASC among patients

with rheumatic disease using a comprehensive EHR-based definition. We observed significant

improvements in the risk of PASC over time and that the risk of PASC may vary according to

rheumatic disease. As current treatment for PASC is primarily supportive based on symptoms,

further work elucidating the underlying pathophysiology of PASC will be helpful to identify

potential targeted treatments. Our findings identify important avenues for future investigation,

including determining the attribution of ongoing symptoms to COVID-19 infection, better

elucidating the proportion with severe outcomes (e.g., myocardial infarction, thromboembolism)

following COVID-19 infection, and determining the risk of rheumatic disease flare following

COVID-19 infection.
